questions.q: What is a watermark in an incremental load?
options: A visual mark added to exported files
The highest already-loaded value of an ordering column, usually a date
A password used to authenticate the pipeline
A checksum of the entire source file
questions.explain: The watermark tracks how far a previous run already loaded, so the next run can start after it.

questions.q: Which column does this lesson use as the watermark column for orders.csv?
options: customer_id
status
order_date
region
questions.explain: order_date is a real column in orders.csv, well suited to tracking which rows are new.

questions.q: What does parse_dates=["order_date"] do in pd.read_csv()?
options: It deletes rows with invalid dates
It parses that column as real datetime64 values instead of plain strings
It sorts the DataFrame by that column
It renames the column
questions.explain: Without parse_dates, comparing a watermark against a plain string column wouldn't compare dates correctly.

questions.q: Why must the watermark only be updated after a successful load, not before?
options: It makes no difference either way
Updating it first is required by pandas
If updated before a failed load, those rows would appear already-loaded and be skipped forever on the next run
SQLite requires watermarks to update before any write
questions.explain: Advancing the watermark too early risks silently losing rows if the load step fails partway through.

questions.q: What does read_watermark() return if no watermark file exists yet?
options: An error that stops the script
The current date
A very old default date, like 1900-01-01, so the first run loads everything
None, causing extract_incremental() to fail
questions.explain: Returning a very early default date ensures the very first run treats every row as new.
